title: How to Write a Vivid Vision: The Complete Guide
metaTitle: How to Write a Vivid Vision (Complete Guide)
metaDescription: A step by step guide to writing a Vivid Vision: a three year picture of your business and life that your team can actually see and build toward.
description: A step by step guide to writing a Vivid Vision: a three year picture of your business and life that your team can actually see and build toward.
keywords: how to write a vivid vision
author: Jennifer Hudye

featuredImage.alt: How to Write a Vivid Vision: The Complete Guide. Article by Jennifer Hudye of Vision Driven.

faq.q: What is a Vivid Vision?
faq.a: A Vivid Vision is a detailed picture of your business and your life three years from now, written in the present tense as if it has already happened. It uses plain language and word pictures so anyone on your team can read it and see the same future you see.

faq.q: How is a Vivid Vision different from a vision board or a business plan?
faq.a: A vision board is pictures with no plan behind it. A business plan is mostly numbers and how-to. A Vivid Vision sits in between. It describes what your company looks like, sounds like, and feels like in three years, in enough detail that your team can act on it, and it covers your life too, not just the business.

faq.q: Why three years and not one year or ten?
faq.a: One year is too close to feel big. You just extend what you are already doing. Ten years is too far to feel real, so your brain stops taking it seriously. Three years is far enough to dream past your current limits, and close enough that you can feel the pull of it on a Monday morning.

faq.q: Do I write about my business, my life, or both?
faq.a: Both, in one document. Most planning splits them apart. That is the whole reason it never sticks. When you build your business vision and your life vision together, every decision in the business starts moving you toward the life you actually want, instead of away from it.

faq.q: How long does it take to write one?
faq.a: A first draft can come out of a focused two day process, or a single VIP day with someone who knows how to pull it out of you. Refining the language and designing the final document takes a few more weeks. Then the real work starts: the rollout.

faq.q: What do I do with it once it is written?
faq.a: You do not put it in a drawer. You read it out loud to your team. You hand out copies. You let people raise their hand for the pieces they want to own. A Vivid Vision that never leaves your laptop was never really finished.

body:
Most founders can tell you their revenue target for next year. Ask them what their company looks like in three years, in detail, and most of them go quiet.

Not because they have not thought about it. Because they have never been asked to write it down in a way anyone else could actually see.

That is what a Vivid Vision is for. And it is the first thing I sit down and build with almost every founder who calls me.

What a Vivid Vision actually is

A Vivid Vision is a picture of your business and your life, three years from now, written in the present tense as if it has already happened.

Not a mood board. Not a list of revenue goals. A real, specific description: what your office feels like when you walk in, what your team is doing without you in the room, what a Tuesday looks like for you personally, what clients say about you, what the money situation actually looks like.

You write it as though you are standing inside that future, looking around, and describing what you see.

Here is the part almost nobody tells you: the value is not in predicting the future correctly. It is in getting specific enough that your brain, and your team's brains, start pulling toward it instead of just drifting.

Why three years, not one and not ten

One year is too close. You just stretch what you are already doing a little further. It does not force you to think differently.

Ten years is too far. It stops feeling real. Your brain quietly files it under fantasy and stops taking it seriously.

Three years sits in the sweet spot. Far enough that you have to think past your current limits, your current team, your current bottlenecks. Close enough that you can feel it pulling on you this Monday.

I have watched this play out with client after client. Akram, who runs the jewelry brand Nominal in Phoenix, built his three year Vivid Vision at a point when the business was messy and barely profitable. Three years later, revenue had tripled and profit had quadrupled. Not because the number three is magic. Because three years was close enough to build toward and far enough to actually dream in.

The mistake almost every founder makes first

Before we get into how to write one, let's clear out the two things people usually try first, because both of them quietly fail.

The first is the vision board. Pictures on a wall, or a Pinterest board, with no mechanism connecting them to a plan. It feels good for about a week. Then life gets busy and the board becomes wallpaper.

The second is the traditional business plan. All numbers, all strategy, zero soul. It might satisfy a bank or an investor. It will not get you out of bed excited, and it definitely will not get your team excited, because there is nothing in it about the actual human beings involved.

A Vivid Vision is built to avoid both traps. It is specific enough to act on, and human enough to actually want.

Fusing your business and your life into one document

Here is the part that changes everything, and it is the whole reason Vision Driven exists.

Most planning fixes your business or your personal life, but rarely both at once. That is exactly why it never sticks.

Think about how most strategic planning actually happens. The founder locks themselves in a room, or takes the team on a retreat, and builds a plan entirely about the business. Revenue. Headcount. Product roadmap. Not one line about whether the founder ever sees their kids, or takes a real vacation, or feels excited to open their laptop.

So the business plan works, if you're lucky, and the founder is still miserable. Hit the number, still stuck. That is the trap Dan, who runs Liquor License Advisor out of Connecticut, was living in before he built his vision. He had sold his house, moved onto a boat, and let the business drift because nothing tied his life goals to his business decisions. Once he built one document that held both, he told me every decision he makes now runs through that same picture.

When you build the business vision and the life vision together, in one process, something shifts. Every decision you make in the business starts moving you toward the life you actually want, instead of quietly working against it.

The Vivid Vision Method, stage by stage

This is the facilitated process we run with founders. You can do a rough version of it yourself. Here is the shape of it.

Stage 1: Vivid Vision Clarity

Before any writing happens, you get clear on where you actually are and where you want to go. We use a mind map and a set of intake questions to stretch your thinking past what feels realistic today.

Every part of the business and the life gets its own branch: team, clients, revenue, product, your health, your family, your calendar, your own state of mind. For each branch, ask the same question: three years from now, at its best, what does this look like?

Do not edit yourself here. Do not ask “how.” The how comes later. Right now you are just painting.

Stage 2: The Vivid Vision Expander

This is the deep session, one focused day, or two to three shorter virtual ones, where you push past your first answers. Whatever you wrote for each branch, ask “and what else?” three more times.

The first answer is usually the safe one. The fourth answer is usually the true one. This is also where a facilitator earns their keep, because it is very hard to expand your own vision past your own ceiling.

Stage 3: Powerfully Articulate Your Vision

Now the vision gets written, in prose. Present tense. First person. Specific enough that someone reading it could picture the actual room, the actual conversation, the actual number on the screen.

This is the stage where most people freeze up on their own, because writing it well feels hard. It does not need to be beautiful. It needs to be clear and specific. “We have a strong team” is not a Vivid Vision. “Sarah runs client onboarding without me touching it, and our new-client satisfaction score has not dropped below nine out of ten in six months” is.

Stage 4: Vision Alive Imagery

Once the words are right, the vision gets designed: an on-brand document, plus a one page Vivid Vision Blueprint and a core values piece you can put on the wall. This is the version that keeps the vision in front of you day to day, so it does not disappear into a folder.

Stage 5: The Vivid Vision Rollout

This is the stage that separates a Vivid Vision that works from one that quietly dies in a drawer. You share it with your team, your partners, and sometimes your clients, and you build it into how the company actually runs. We will spend a whole section on it below, because it deserves one.

The questions that actually open up a real Vivid Vision

If you want to try a rough first pass yourself, sit down somewhere quiet and answer these out loud, or write them by hand. Present tense. Three years out.

  • What does a normal Tuesday look like for you? Where are you. What are you doing. What are you not doing anymore.
  • Who is on your team, and what are they doing without you checking their work?
  • What are clients saying about you, in their own words?
  • What does the money actually look like? Not just revenue. What is left over, and what is it doing for you?
  • What have you stopped doing that you used to spend hours on every week?
  • Where do you travel, and who is with you?
  • What is the one thing people in your industry now say about your company that they did not used to say?

Notice none of these ask “how.” That question comes after the vision is written, not before. Answering “how” too early is the fastest way to shrink your vision down to whatever feels achievable today, which defeats the entire point.

What actually goes inside the document

People get stuck on the blank page because nobody tells them what the sections are. Here is a simple structure that works for almost any company.

The team

Who is on it. How big it is. What the culture feels like on a normal day. What people say about working there. What roles exist now that do not exist today. And the big one: what is the team doing well without you in the room?

The clients

Who you serve, and who you have stopped serving. What they say about you in their own words. How they find you. What the experience of working with you feels like from their side.

The offer and the marketing

What you sell three years from now. How people hear about you. What your reputation is in the market, said in one sentence, the way someone at a conference would describe you to a friend.

The money

Not just revenue. Profit margin. What is in the bank. What the business pays you, and what that money is doing for your life. Whether you are funding growth from cash flow or something else.

Operations and systems

What runs without you. What used to be a fire and is now boring and predictable. The three or four systems that make the whole thing hold together.

Your role

What you spend your days doing. What you have handed off. What only you do, on purpose, because it is your zone of genius and nobody should take it from you.

Your life

Your health. Your family. Your calendar. Where you live and where you travel. What a Sunday looks like. How you feel when you wake up on a work day. This section is not optional, and it is not last. Write it with the same detail as the revenue section.

You do not need every section to be long. You need every section to be specific. One vivid, true sentence beats a paragraph of corporate filler.

A short example, so you can see the difference

Here is a weak version of a team section, the kind most founders write on their first try:

We have a great team that is aligned around our mission. Everyone is bought in and takes ownership. We have hired A players in every seat.

Now here is a vivid version of the same idea:

Our team is sixteen people. Maria runs operations and I have not been in a delivery meeting in four months. New hires say their first week felt organized, because we finally wrote the onboarding down. Nobody works past six unless they choose to. When something breaks, the person closest to it fixes it and tells me after, instead of waiting for me to decide.

Same message. One of them your team can picture and build toward. The other one is a mission statement nobody remembers by lunch.

Do that for every section. Trade the adjectives for a specific picture.

Five mistakes that kill a Vivid Vision before it starts

I have watched hundreds of founders attempt this. The ones who stall out almost always hit one of these.

Writing it alone in your head, never on paper. If it is not written down in detail, it is not a Vivid Vision. It is a mood.

Making it only about the business. Skip your life and the vision will not survive contact with a hard quarter, because there is nothing personal pulling you through it.

Playing it safe. If your three year vision only stretches a little past where you are now, you wrote a budget, not a vision.

Never sharing it with your team. More on this below. This one alone kills most visions.

Writing it once and never looking at it again. A vision you open once a year does not change your decisions. It has to stay in front of you.

The part almost everyone skips: the rollout

Here is something I tell every client, and it still surprises most of them: writing the Vivid Vision is not the hard part. Sharing it is.

Stacy, co-founder of Share One in Austin, told me she and her husband almost stopped at the written document. They figured it was something to put on the wall for the two of them. It never occurred to them to share it with their team.

Once they did, hand mailing printed vision packets to a team spread across the country and opening them together on a call, something shifted. People started raising their hands for pieces of the vision they wanted to own. The culture got tighter. And within three years, the company hit every benchmark they had written down, plus two unprompted investor conversations that matched a line item from the original vision.

Your team cannot align around a picture they have never seen. If you are the only one who knows where the company is headed, you are also the only one making decisions, which is exactly the trap that keeps founders stuck working fifty hours a week for a business that cannot run without them.

Share it with your team. Share it with your investors if you have them. Read it out loud at least once. Let people ask questions about it. Let people volunteer for the parts that excite them.

Here is a simple rollout format that works. Get the team together, in a room or on a call. Give everyone a printed copy. Read it out loud yourself, start to finish, no slides. Then go section by section and ask two questions: what part of this are you most excited about, and what part do you want to own? Write down what people say. Follow up within a week.

That is it. You are not selling them on it. You are letting them see the same picture you see, and giving them a way in.

Keeping it alive after the first read

A Vivid Vision that gets written once and filed away is worse than no vision at all, because now you also feel guilty about it.

Keeping it alive is a rhythm, not an event. A few things that work:

  • Put the one page version somewhere you actually look. Not a folder. A wall, a desktop background, the first page of your planning doc.
  • Read the full document out loud once a quarter, by yourself, before you plan the next ninety days. It takes ten minutes and it re-points your compass.
  • Every quarter, break one slice of the three year vision into a ninety day goal. This is where the vision connects to your actual calendar. It is the difference between a nice document and a plan you are walking toward.
  • Once a year, rewrite it. Not from scratch. But your life changes, the business changes, and a vision you never update slowly stops being true.

The quarterly step is the one that matters most. A three year picture with nothing connecting it to this week is just a poster. Breaking it down every ninety days is how it turns into decisions.

What actually changes when you do this for real

I am not going to tell you a Vivid Vision guarantees a specific result. Anyone who promises you a number is not being straight with you.

What I can tell you, from watching this play out with hundreds of founders, is what tends to change. Decisions get faster, because you are checking them against a picture instead of debating from scratch every time. Your team starts bringing you solutions instead of problems, because they know what you are building toward. And the split between “growing the business” and “having a life” starts to close, because you built both into the same document instead of sacrificing one for the other.

That is the whole point. Not a prettier plan. A different way of making every decision from here forward.

But you do not have time to step away and do this

I hear this from almost every founder, and I understand it. Your calendar is full. Stepping away for two days to write a document feels like a luxury you cannot afford right now.

Here is the thing I have watched play out over and over. If you cannot step away from the business for two days, that is not a reason to skip this. That is the clearest sign you need it.

A business that cannot survive two days without you is not a business yet. It is a job you cannot quit. And the way out of that is not working more hours. It is getting a clear enough picture of where you are headed that your team can start making decisions without you, which is the only thing that ever actually buys back your time.

Clarity does not cost you time. Lack of it does. Every month you spend without a clear direction is a month of your team asking you questions they could have answered themselves, a month of projects that drift because nobody is sure they matter, a month of you being the bottleneck.

The two days are not the expensive part. The years of drift are.

How this changes as the company grows

A founder with a five person team and a founder with a fifty person team both need a Vivid Vision. What changes is the rollout.

At five people, you can get everyone in a room, read it out loud, and have a real conversation about it in an afternoon. Everyone hears it from you directly.

At fifty, you cannot do that in one sitting, and you should not try. You share it with your leadership team first, in depth. They sit with it, ask their hard questions, and get to a place where they can speak to it in their own words. Then each of them rolls it out to their part of the company. The vision travels through your leaders, not around them.

The document itself does not need to get longer as you grow. If anything it should get tighter. What grows is the care you put into how it reaches people.

Where to start

If you want to try a rough draft yourself, block two hours, use the questions above, and write in present tense. Do not edit as you go.

If you would rather have someone pull it out of you properly, in a day, with a process built for exactly this, that is the work I do with founders through a Vivid Vision engagement. You can read more about how the whole approach fits together, or see what it actually looked like for founders who have been through it.

Hold the vision. Not the circumstances.

title: Founder Impostor Syndrome: Why It Gets Worse the More You Succeed
metaTitle: Founder Impostor Syndrome: Why Success Makes It Worse
metaDescription: Why impostor syndrome gets louder as your business grows, and what actually helps a successful founder stop feeling like a fraud.
description: Why impostor syndrome gets louder as your business grows, and what actually helps a successful founder stop feeling like a fraud.
author: Jennifer Hudye

featuredImage.alt: Founder Impostor Syndrome: Why It Gets Worse the More You Succeed. Article by Jennifer Hudye of Vision Driven.

faq.q: Why does impostor syndrome get worse as a founder succeeds, instead of better?
faq.a: Because every new level of success raises the height of the fall in your own mind. Early on you can blame luck or timing. Once you have real proof you are good at this, the only story left is that you have not been caught yet, which feels scarier, not safer.

faq.q: Is impostor syndrome common among founders?
faq.a: In my experience, almost every founder I have worked with has felt it at some point, including the ones who look the most confident from the outside. It is closer to the default than the exception.

faq.q: Does impostor syndrome ever fully go away?
faq.a: For most founders, it does not disappear. It gets quieter once you have a clear picture of who you are becoming, not just what you have already built, so the feeling stops running the show even when it shows up.

faq.q: What is the identity mismatch behind impostor syndrome?
faq.a: It is the gap between who you believe you are and who you are actually becoming. When your business grows faster than your self-image, the growth itself starts to feel unearned, even when the results are real.

faq.q: How is this connected to having a Vivid Vision?
faq.a: A Vivid Vision gives you a picture of the founder you are growing into, not just a revenue target. That picture becomes something to grow into on purpose, instead of feeling like you are getting away with something.

body:
You would think the further along a founder gets, the quieter that voice in their head would get.

It is usually the opposite.

I have sat across from founders doing seven and eight figures, people other entrepreneurs quietly study and try to copy, who told me some version of the same sentence: I feel like I am about to get caught.

Why success makes it louder, not quieter

Early on, it is almost easy to explain away a win. You got lucky. You had a good month. The market was hot.

But once you have three years of results behind you, once the wins are too consistent to blame on luck, that excuse stops working. And when the excuse stops working, something uncomfortable happens: the only story left is that you have not been caught yet.

Success does not resolve impostor syndrome. It raises the height of the fall.

The identity mismatch nobody names

Here is what is actually happening underneath it, in plain terms.

Your business grew. Your team grew. Your revenue grew. And your picture of yourself did not keep up.

You are still, somewhere in your head, running the story of who you were three years ago: the person figuring it out, winging half of it, hoping nobody looked too closely. Except that person is not who is actually running the company anymore. The gap between the old story and the current reality is where impostor syndrome lives.

It is not a character flaw. It is a founder whose identity has not caught up to their own results.

Why “just be more confident” does not work

Most advice on this topic tells you to think positive, or fake it until you make it, or remember your wins.

In my experience, that rarely holds for more than a week, because it treats the symptom, not the gap. Reminding yourself of your wins does not close the distance between who you think you are and who you are actually becoming. It just adds another fact to argue with the feeling, and the feeling usually wins that argument at 11pm.

What actually helps is closing the gap itself. Not by lowering your results. By raising your picture of who you are.

The moments that set it off

Impostor syndrome does not hum along at a steady volume. It spikes. And it spikes at predictable moments, usually the good ones.

Hiring someone more credentialed than you. Now there is a person on payroll who went to the school you did not, or ran the department you have only read about, and they report to you. Your brain says: they are going to figure out I do not know what I am doing.

Getting press, or getting on a stage. Suddenly you are being introduced as an expert, in front of people, and the gap between the introduction and how you feel on the inside is loud.

Landing a client or a partner who is a bigger name than you expected to be working with yet. Instead of feeling proud, you feel like you tricked them.

Watching a peer succeed. Someone at your level, or slightly ahead, hits a milestone, and instead of being happy for them you feel behind, exposed, like the clock is running out.

Notice the pattern. None of these are failures. They are all evidence that things are going well. The feeling is not a response to danger. It is a response to growth your identity has not caught up to.

Impostor syndrome is not the same as a real skills gap

This matters, so I want to be careful with it.

Impostor syndrome is feeling like a fraud when the evidence says you are not one. You have the results, the clients, the team, and you still feel like it is going to come apart. That is the identity gap, and the fix is the inner work in this article.

A real skills gap is different. That is when there is an actual thing you do not know how to do yet, and it is genuinely holding the business back. Reading financials. Hiring well. Having hard conversations. The fix for that is not a mindset shift. It is learning the skill, or hiring someone who has it.

Most founders have some of both. The trick is to be honest about which is which. Do not use real gaps as proof you are a fraud. And do not use the word impostor to avoid learning something you actually need to learn.

What actually helps

This is where a real, written picture of where you are headed does something that a pep talk cannot.

When you sit down and write a three year Vivid Vision, in detail, in the present tense, you are not just describing a bigger business. You are describing a bigger version of yourself: the leader who runs that team, who makes those decisions, who is respected in that specific way.

You start growing into that person on purpose, instead of accidentally outgrowing your old self-image and feeling like a fraud every time reality moves faster than your identity does.

This is part of what we call the Big Life Stages of Entrepreneurship: the shift from an achievement driven stage, where you are chasing the next number and it never feels like enough, to a vision driven stage, where your decisions come from a clear picture of who you are building toward. Impostor syndrome tends to live hardest in that gap between the two stages.

A few things that help in the meantime, while that identity catches up:

  • Say the feeling out loud to one person you trust. It loses power the moment it is not a secret anymore.
  • Keep a short list of decisions only you could have made well. Not wins. Decisions. It rebuilds the evidence base your identity is missing.
  • Stop comparing your inside to someone else's outside. Every founder who looks certain from the stage has felt exactly what you are feeling right now.
  • Get your vision out of your head and onto paper. Vague fear stays loud. A specific picture of where you are headed gives your brain somewhere else to put its attention.

The Golden Jail Cell connection

There is a specific flavor of this that shows up in founders who are stuck in what I call the Golden Jail Cell: a business too big to walk away from, but too dependent on you to give you any freedom.

Impostor syndrome and the Golden Jail Cell feed each other. You do not trust the team enough to let go, because some part of you is not sure you deserve the company you built in the first place. So you hold on tighter, which proves to your team you do not trust them, which keeps the business dependent on you, which keeps you exhausted, which makes the whole thing feel even less earned.

The way out of both is the same: a clear vision of the founder you are becoming, one confident enough to let other people own real pieces of the business, written down specifically enough that you can start acting like that person before you fully feel like them.

You are not behind

If you are running a real business, with real revenue, real clients, and a real team, and you still feel like you are getting away with something, you are not broken and you are not behind.

You are a founder whose identity has not caught up to your results yet. That is fixable. It is not fixed by trying harder to feel confident. It is fixed by getting specific about who you are growing into, and building toward that person on purpose.

Hold the vision. Not the circumstances.

title: What Is the Vision Driven Method? Why Most Business Plans Fail Without It
metaTitle: What Is the Vision Driven Method?
metaDescription: The Vision Driven Method fuses your business plan and your life plan into one process. Here is what it is, why it works, and how to start using it.
description: The Vision Driven Method fuses your business plan and your life plan into one process. Here is what it is, why it works, and how to start using it.
category: Turn Your Vision Into a Plan
author: Jennifer Hudye

faq.q: What is the Vision Driven Method?
faq.a: It is a single operating system that fuses your personal life and your business strategy into one planning process, instead of treating them as two separate documents that never talk to each other.

faq.q: How is this different from normal quarterly planning?
faq.a: Normal quarterly planning is almost always business-only: revenue, headcount, product. The Vision Driven Method starts with your personal life first, then reverse engineers the business quarter from it, so the plan actually serves the life you want instead of quietly working against it.

faq.q: Do I need a written Vivid Vision before I can use this?
faq.a: It helps a great deal. The Vivid Vision gives you the three year picture. The Vision Driven Method is how you break that picture into a quarter you can actually act on this month.

faq.a: Founders who have hit their revenue targets and still feel stuck, or founders who keep building great quarters for the business while their personal life quietly falls apart in the background.

faq.a: Before you plan a single business goal for next quarter, write down what you want true in your personal life at the end of it. Then build the business quarter around protecting that, not around ignoring it.

body:
Here is a pattern I have seen more times than I can count. A founder hits every number on their business plan for the quarter. Revenue is up. The team delivered. By any normal measure, it was a good quarter.

And the founder is exhausted, distant from their family, and quietly dreading the next one.

The plan worked. The founder did not. That gap is exactly what the Vision Driven Method is built to close.

What the Vision Driven Method actually is

The Vision Driven Method is a single approach that fuses your personal clarity and your business strategy into one process, instead of running them as two separate tracks that never talk to each other.

Most planning splits them apart on purpose. There is the business plan, built in a room with spreadsheets and revenue targets. And there is, if you are lucky, some vague idea of “work-life balance” floating around in the background, never actually written down or built into the plan.

The Vision Driven Method puts both in the same document, built in the same sitting, so neither one gets to quietly cannibalize the other.

Why splitting them apart is the actual problem

Business plans and life plans built apart from each other pull the founder in two directions. Built together, they compound.

When your life goals live nowhere on paper, they lose every negotiation against a business deadline. There is no meeting where “I want to be home for dinner” gets to compete with a client emergency, because it was never written down as a real priority in the first place. It just quietly loses, every time, by default.

The Vision Driven Method forces both into the room together, so a quarter that hits its revenue number but wrecks your health or your marriage does not get to count as a win anymore.

How it actually works

The order matters more than most founders expect.

Step 1: Start with the life, not the business

Before a single business goal gets written down, go back to your three year Vivid Vision and answer this: three years from now, what do I want to be true about my health, my family, my own state of mind? Then narrow it down. Which slice of that am I moving this quarter?

Most founders have never written the life side down at the start of a planning cycle. It usually shows up, if at all, as a vague afterthought at the end.

Step 2: Reverse engineer the business quarter from there

Now ask: given what I just wrote, what does the business need from me this quarter, and just as important, what does it not need from me?

This single question kills more busywork than any productivity system I have ever seen. A lot of what feels urgent in a normal business plan quietly disappears once it has to justify itself against the life you actually want.

Step 3: Set your quarterly rocks

Pick three to five priorities for the quarter. Not fifteen. Three to five. If everything is a priority, nothing is.

Each rock should serve both tracks: the business outcome, and the life outcome from step one. If a goal only serves the business and actively works against the life you want, question whether it belongs in this quarter at all.

Step 4: Build your rhythm

A quarter without a rhythm turns into fifty scattered decisions instead of one clear direction. Set your check-in cadence now: weekly for the team, monthly for yourself, so the plan does not just live in a document nobody reopens until the next planning session.

Step 5: Build a scoreboard that includes your life

Most business scoreboards track revenue, pipeline, and delivery. Very few track whether you actually took the vacation you planned, or whether you made it to the things that mattered outside of work.

Put both on the same scoreboard. What gets measured gets protected. What only lives in your head gets sacrificed the first time things get busy.

What this looks like in a real quarter

Akram, who runs Nominal, told me one of the biggest shifts was realizing his firefighting was not actually the job. Once his planning started from the life he wanted, including real time with his newborn daughter, the business quarter around it looked completely different. Different hires. Different priorities. Fewer fires, because fewer of them were actually his to put out in the first place.

That is the whole mechanism. The plan does not get softer. It gets more honest about what it is actually for.

How this compares to the planning systems you already know

If you run a business, you have probably touched one of the common operating systems: a quarterly rocks model, an objectives and key results model, or a simple annual plan broken into quarters. These are good tools. Millions of companies use them well.

Here is the one thing almost all of them have in common: they are built to run a company, not a life. The templates ask about revenue, about departmental goals, about the number. There is usually no line on the page that asks what you want to be true about your health or your family at the end of the quarter.

The Vision Driven Method is not a replacement for those tools. If your rocks model works for your team, keep it. What changes is the input. Before you fill in the business template, you write the life side first, and then the business quarter has to fit around it instead of the other way around.

You can run this on top of whatever system your company already uses. It is a change in what you decide first, not a change in your software.

A week of actually running it

People ask what this looks like day to day. It is lighter than it sounds.

Monday morning, before anything else, you look at your three to five rocks for the quarter and pick what moves this week. Ten minutes.

Midweek, your team has its normal check-in. The only change is that one of the things you track out loud is whether the founder is on track for the life side, not just the business side. It sounds strange the first few times. Then it becomes normal, and people start protecting your calendar without being asked.

Friday, you spend fifteen minutes on two questions. What moved this week. What did I let pull me off the plan, and was it worth it. You are not grading yourself. You are keeping the plan honest.

Once a month, you take an hour by yourself and look at the whole quarter. Are the rocks still the right rocks. Is the life side actually happening, or did it quietly get traded away again. If it got traded away, that is the real problem to solve, not a footnote.

The mistake that undoes all of this

The Vision Driven Method fails the same way every planning system fails: when it only gets used once and then forgotten.

A quarterly plan built with real intention and then never looked at again is not a system. It is a nice memory from a planning offsite.

Put your rocks somewhere you see them weekly. Review the life side of the plan with the same seriousness as the revenue side. If a quarter is going sideways on the life side, treat that as a real signal, the same way you would treat missing a revenue number, not as something to quietly ignore until burnout forces the conversation.

Where this fits with your Vivid Vision

If you already have a three year Vivid Vision written, the Vision Driven Method is how you break it into something you can actually act on this quarter. The Vivid Vision is the picture on the wall. The Vision Driven Method is how you build the next ninety days to walk toward it.

If you have not written your three year vision yet, start there. A quarterly plan with no destination behind it just optimizes whatever you are already doing, a little faster.

You can read more about how the two connect on the Frameworks page, or see how it played out for real founders on Case Studies.

Hold the vision. Not the circumstances.

title: What Is a Vivid Vision? A Plain-English Guide With Examples
metaTitle: What Is a Vivid Vision? (Plain-English Guide)
metaDescription: A Vivid Vision is a present-tense picture of your business and life three years out. Here is what it is, what goes in it, and how it is different from a business plan.
description: A Vivid Vision is a present-tense picture of your business and life three years out. Here is what it is, what goes in it, and how it is different from a business plan.
author: Jennifer Hudye

featuredImage.alt: What Is a Vivid Vision? A Plain-English Guide With Examples. Article by Jennifer Hudye of Vision Driven.

faq.q: What is a Vivid Vision in simple terms?
faq.a: It is a written picture of your business and your life three years from now, in the present tense, as if it has already happened. It is specific enough that anyone on your team can read it and see the same future you see.

faq.q: Who created the Vivid Vision idea?
faq.a: The Vivid Vision came from Cameron Herold, author of the book Vivid Vision. Jennifer Hudye has partnered with him since 2016 and has guided more than 550 companies through the process.

faq.q: How is a Vivid Vision different from a vision statement?
faq.a: A vision statement is usually one line on a wall that nobody remembers. A Vivid Vision is three to five pages of specific, present-tense detail about the team, the clients, the money, the operations, and your own life.

faq.q: How far out should a Vivid Vision go?
faq.a: Three years. One year is too close to change your thinking. Ten years stops feeling real. Three years is far enough to dream past your current limits and close enough to start building toward on Monday.

faq.q: Does a Vivid Vision include personal life or just the business?
faq.a: Both, in one document. That is the whole point. Most planning splits them apart, which is why neither one sticks.

body:
Ask ten founders what a Vivid Vision is and you will get ten different answers. Some think it is a fancy mission statement. Some think it is a vision board. Some think it is a business plan with nicer fonts.

None of those are quite right.

The short definition

A Vivid Vision is a written picture of your business and your life three years from now, in the present tense, as if it has already happened.

You describe what the company looks like, sounds like, and feels like. What your team is doing without you in the room. What clients say about you in their own words. What the money situation actually is. And what a normal day looks like for you personally.

It is usually three to five pages. It is specific. And it is written so that anyone can read it and see the same future you see.

Where the idea comes from

The Vivid Vision came from Cameron Herold, the author of the book Vivid Vision. Jennifer Hudye has partnered with him since 2016, and her team has guided more than 550 companies through the process since then.

The core belief behind it is simple. People and teams move toward a picture they can see. A vague goal pulls no one forward. A vivid, specific picture of the future does.

What a Vivid Vision is not

It is not a one line vision statement. Those live on a wall and change nobody’s decisions.

It is not a vision board. Pictures with no plan behind them feel good for a week, then become wallpaper.

It is not a traditional business plan. A business plan is built for a bank or an investor. It is all numbers and strategy, with nothing in it about the humans involved or the life the business is supposed to fund.

A Vivid Vision sits in between all of those. Specific enough to act on. Human enough to actually want.

What goes inside it

A strong Vivid Vision covers, at minimum:

  • The team. Who is on it, how big it is, what the culture feels like, and what the team is handling well without you.
  • The clients. Who you serve, what they say about you, and what the experience feels like from their side.
  • The offer and the marketing. What you sell in three years and how people hear about you.
  • The money. Not just revenue. Profit, cash in the bank, and what the business pays you.
  • Operations. What runs without you. What used to be a fire and is now boring and predictable.
  • Your role. What you spend your days doing, and what you have handed off.
  • Your life. Health, family, calendar, travel, and how you feel when you wake up on a work day.

That last one is not optional, and it does not go at the end. Write it with the same care as the revenue section.

Why the personal side matters

Most planning fixes your business or your personal life, but rarely both at once. That is exactly why it never sticks.

When your life goals are not written anywhere, they lose every negotiation against a business deadline. When they are written into the same document as the business plan, every business decision starts moving you toward the life you actually want, instead of away from it.

How it gets built

The full process is the Vivid Vision Method: Vivid Vision Clarity, the Vivid Vision Expander, Powerfully Articulate Your Vision, Vision Alive Imagery, and the Vivid Vision Rollout. You can also do a rough first draft yourself in a couple of hours. There is a full walkthrough in how to write a Vivid Vision.

If you want to see what a finished one looks like, read Vivid Vision examples. And if you want the difference spelled out, here is Vivid Vision versus a mission statement versus a business plan.

Why present tense, and why it feels strange

A Vivid Vision is written as if the three years have already passed. It is December of that year and our team is twenty people, not we will grow to twenty people.

Your brain treats will and hope to as someday, and someday never organizes your Tuesday. Present tense removes the escape hatch. It forces your mind to build the picture as real, and then it starts closing the gap between that picture and today without being told to.

The first page feels like you are making things up. By the second page most people stop noticing. If it still feels fake after a full page, you are probably describing what you think you should want instead of what you actually want. Back up and get honest.

A weak line versus a vivid line

Weak: we have a strong, aligned team that takes ownership.

Vivid: our team is sixteen people. Maria runs operations and I have not joined a delivery meeting in four months. When something breaks, the person closest to it fixes it and tells me after.

Same idea. One your team can picture and build toward. The other is a slogan nobody remembers by lunch. Every section of a strong Vivid Vision passes that test: trade the adjectives for a specific scene, a number, or a named outcome.

How to start this week

Block two hours somewhere quiet. Set a date three years out at the top of a blank page. Then write, section by section, in the present tense, using the prompts in questions to ask before you write your company vision. Do not edit as you go. Do not ask how. The how comes after the picture exists.

When the draft is done, that is the beginning, not the end. The full process is the Vivid Vision Method, and the part that actually changes your company is the rollout to your team.

The one thing people get wrong

They write it, feel good about it, and never share it. A Vivid Vision that never leaves your laptop was never really finished. The rollout to your team is where it starts changing anything.

Hold the vision. Not the circumstances.

title: Vivid Vision vs. Mission Statement vs. Business Plan
metaTitle: Vivid Vision vs. Mission Statement vs. Business Plan
metaDescription: How a Vivid Vision is different from a mission statement and a business plan, and when to use each one.
description: How a Vivid Vision is different from a mission statement and a business plan, and when to use each one.
author: Jennifer Hudye

featuredImage.alt: Vivid Vision vs. Mission Statement vs. Business Plan. Article by Jennifer Hudye of Vision Driven.

faq.q: Do I need a mission statement if I have a Vivid Vision?
faq.a: They do different jobs. A mission statement says why the company exists in one line. A Vivid Vision describes where it is going in detail. Most companies keep a short mission line and build a Vivid Vision underneath it.

faq.q: Is a Vivid Vision a replacement for a business plan?
faq.a: No. A business plan handles the numbers, the model, and the strategy. A Vivid Vision handles the picture of the future that the plan is trying to reach. They work together.

faq.q: Which one do I write first?
faq.a: The Vivid Vision. It tells you where you are going. The business plan is then built to get you there. Writing the plan first tends to shrink the vision down to whatever looks achievable today.

faq.q: Can a small company have a Vivid Vision?
faq.a: Yes. It matters most once you have a team, because a shared picture of the future is what lets your team make decisions without you.

body:
Founders use these three terms like they are the same thing. They are not, and mixing them up is why a lot of companies have a vision that changes nothing.

Mission statement

A mission statement answers one question: why does this company exist?

It is short. One or two sentences. It does not change much over the years. It is useful as a filter for big decisions, and it is close to useless for aligning a team on where you are headed next, because it does not describe a destination.

Keep one. Keep it short. Do not expect it to do the job of a vision.

Business plan

A business plan answers: how will this company make money, and what is the strategy?

It is numbers, models, market analysis, and a roadmap. It is built for a bank, an investor, or your own financial planning. It is precise and it is dry.

A business plan is the wrong tool for getting your team excited or for connecting the company to your personal life, because neither of those things belongs in a financial document.

Vivid Vision

A Vivid Vision answers: what does this company, and my life, look like in three years?

It is three to five pages, written in the present tense, describing the team, the clients, the money, the operations, your role, and your life, as if you are standing in that future looking around.

It is specific enough to act on and human enough to actually want. It is the destination the business plan is trying to reach.

How they fit together

Think of it as three layers.

  • Mission is why you exist. It rarely changes.
  • Vivid Vision is where you are going over the next three years. You rewrite it roughly once a year.
  • Business plan is how you get there. It changes every quarter.

Most planning fixes your business or your personal life, but rarely both. The Vivid Vision is the one layer built to hold both at once, which is why it is the layer that makes decisions actually change.

The order matters

Write the Vivid Vision first. Then build the business plan to reach it. Then break the plan into a 90-day plan you will actually follow.

Do it the other way around and you will quietly cap your vision at whatever your current spreadsheet says is possible.

Common mix-ups, and why they cost you

Treating the mission as the vision. You put a one-line purpose on the wall and call it done. Your team has nothing to aim at, so every decision comes back to you.

Treating the business plan as the vision. You have a detailed model and forecast, and no picture of the life it is supposed to fund. You hit the numbers and still feel stuck, because most planning fixes your business or your personal life, but rarely both.

Having a vision with no plan under it. A vivid three-year picture and nothing connecting it to this quarter. It floats above the work, admired and ignored.

The fix for all three is to run all three layers on purpose: a short mission, a Vivid Vision you rewrite once a year, and a business plan you break into a 90-day plan every quarter.

When to use each one

Reach for the mission when you are making a values call: should we take this client, enter this market, build this product.

Reach for the Vivid Vision when you are aligning people or making a three-year bet: hiring a leader, setting the direction for the year, deciding what kind of company you are becoming.

Reach for the business plan when you are deciding how to spend the next 90 days and the next dollar.

If you only have one of the three, you will keep using it for jobs it was not built for, and it will keep coming up short.

A quick test

Hand your current vision document to someone who does not work at your company. Ask them to describe what your business looks like in three years.

If they can, you have a Vivid Vision. If they give you a vague sentence back, you have a mission statement wearing a costume. Start with how to write a Vivid Vision.

What each one looks like in practice

Say you run a fifteen-person agency and a client asks you to take on work outside your specialty.

Your mission helps you decide whether to say yes at all. If your reason for existing is to do one thing better than anyone, the mission says no.

Your Vivid Vision helps you decide what to do with the gap. If the three-year picture includes a second service line, this is a nudge to start building it on purpose instead of one custom project at a time.

Your business plan tells you whether you have the margin and the people to take it on this quarter without wrecking your other commitments.

One question, three tools, three different jobs. Founders who only have a business plan answer it purely on this-quarter revenue and end up drifting away from what the company was for.

Why founders skip the Vivid Vision

The mission is easy to write and feels done. The business plan is demanded by banks and investors, so it gets made. The Vivid Vision is the one nobody forces you to do, so it is the one that gets skipped, and it is the one that would have kept the other two aimed at something.

If your company has a mission on the wall and a forecast in a spreadsheet and still feels like it is wandering, the missing layer is almost always the middle one.

A note on the personal layer

Here is the piece none of the three traditional documents handle well. Your life. A mission statement is about the company’s purpose. A business plan is about the company’s money. Neither one has a place to say I am home for dinner four nights a week and I take two real vacations a year.

The Vivid Vision is the only one of the three with room for that, and putting it there is not sentimental. It is structural. When your life is written into the same document as the revenue targets, every strategic decision has to account for it. When it lives nowhere, it loses every close call. That is the real reason the Vivid Vision is the layer that changes how a founder actually lives, not just how the company runs.

Getting all three in place

Keep your mission to one or two sentences. Write your Vivid Vision as three to five present-tense pages covering the business and your life. Then build the business plan to reach it, and break that into a 90-day plan each quarter. That is the full stack, and each layer does a job the others cannot.

Hold the vision. Not the circumstances.

title: Vivid Vision Examples: What a Strong One Actually Looks Like
metaTitle: Vivid Vision Examples (What Good Ones Look Like)
metaDescription: Side-by-side examples of weak versus strong Vivid Vision writing, plus the pattern that makes a vision specific enough for a team to build toward.
description: Side-by-side examples of weak versus strong Vivid Vision writing, plus the pattern that makes a vision specific enough for a team to build toward.
author: Jennifer Hudye

featuredImage.alt: Vivid Vision Examples: What a Strong One Actually Looks Like. Article by Jennifer Hudye of Vision Driven.

faq.q: Are there public Vivid Vision examples I can read?
faq.a: Yes. Cameron Herold has published his own personal Vivid Vision and the one for COO Alliance. Vision Driven has also published example culture packages. The pattern matters more than any single example, though.

faq.q: How long is a typical Vivid Vision?
faq.a: Three to five pages for the written document, plus a one page visual summary called the Vivid Vision Blueprint.

faq.q: Should I copy someone else's Vivid Vision?
faq.a: Copy the structure and the level of detail, never the content. A vision that is not yours will not pull you or your team anywhere.

faq.q: What makes an example strong?
faq.a: Specificity. A strong example lets you picture an actual room, an actual conversation, or an actual number. A weak one is full of adjectives like world-class and mission-driven.

body:
The fastest way to understand a Vivid Vision is to see the difference between a weak one and a strong one, section by section.

The rule underneath every example: trade the adjectives for a specific picture.

Team section

Weak: We have a world-class team that is fully aligned around our mission and takes complete ownership of their work.

Strong: Our team is eighteen people. Priya runs delivery and I have not joined a client call in five months. New hires tell us their first week felt calm because the onboarding is written down and actually followed. When something breaks, the person closest to it fixes it and tells me after.

The strong version is something a team can read and build toward. The weak version is a slogan.

Client section

Weak: Our clients love us and refer us constantly because we deliver exceptional value.

Strong: Clients describe us to their friends as the people who finally made the vision thing click. Two out of every three new clients come from a referral. Nobody has asked for a discount in a year, because the outcome is obvious before they sign.

Money section

Weak: The business is highly profitable and financially healthy with strong margins.

Strong: We run at a 28 percent profit margin. There are six months of operating cash in the bank. The business pays me a salary that covers my life twice over, and I have not personally guaranteed a loan in two years.

Your life section

Weak: I have achieved a healthy work-life balance and feel fulfilled.

Strong: I work four days a week and I am home for dinner every night I am in town. I took two full weeks off in the summer and the business grew while I was gone. I lift three mornings a week and I have not missed one of my daughter’s games this season.

What all the strong versions have in common

  • They use numbers, names, and specific scenes.
  • They describe the team doing things without the founder.
  • They put the founder’s personal life in the same document as the revenue.
  • They are written in the present tense, not I will or we hope to.

Operations section

Weak: our operations are efficient and our processes are well documented.

Strong: onboarding a new client takes two days and follows a checklist anyone on the team can run. We have not missed a delivery date in four months. The thing that used to be a weekly fire, billing, is now boring, because we fixed it in Q2.

Marketing section

Weak: we have a strong brand and a growing audience that trusts us.

Strong: two out of every three new clients come from a referral or from someone who read our writing first. On a sales call we no longer defend our price, because the outcome is obvious before they sign.

How to turn a weak line into a strong one

When you catch an abstract line, run it through three questions:

  • Who is doing it? Name a person or a role, not the company in general.
  • What is the number? Attach a real figure: a margin, a count, a timeframe.
  • What can I picture? Rewrite it as a scene you could actually watch happen.

Do that for every section and the vision goes from a page of adjectives to something your team can build.

How to use an example

Read one, then close it. Do not copy the words. Copy the level of detail and the present-tense voice.

Then write your own, section by section, using the structure in this guide. When you catch yourself writing an adjective like world-class or cutting-edge, stop and describe the actual thing instead.

You can see how this played out for real founders on the case studies page.

The personal section, weak versus strong

Weak: I have found a healthy balance and I feel fulfilled and energized.

Strong: I work four days a week and I am home for dinner every night I am in town. I took two full weeks off in July and the business grew while I was gone. I lift Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, and I have not missed one of my son’s games this season.

This is the section founders write in one vague line and then wonder why the business always wins the close calls. Write it with the same specificity as the revenue section. If you cannot picture it, you have not decided what you actually want yet.

A note on numbers in a Vivid Vision

Specific does not mean you are making a forecast. A number in a Vivid Vision is a texture, not a projection. Twenty-eight percent margin tells your team the company is genuinely profitable and self-funding, in a way that healthy margins never could. Sixteen people tells them the scale you are building for.

Pick numbers that make the picture concrete. You are not committing to hit them to the decimal. You are giving your team something they can actually see.

Two ways to practice

First, take your current vision or mission and rewrite one section using the three questions above: who is doing it, what is the number, what can I picture. Notice how much longer and more useful it gets.

Second, describe your own last great Tuesday from three years ago in present tense, as if it were happening now. That teaches your hand the voice a Vivid Vision is written in. Then do it for the Tuesday you want three years from today.

When you are ready for the full draft, use how to write a Vivid Vision.

Hold the vision. Not the circumstances.

title: Why Your Company Vision Isn't Working (And How to Fix It)
metaTitle: Why Your Company Vision Isn't Working
metaDescription: Five reasons a company vision fails to change anything, and the fix for each one.
description: Five reasons a company vision fails to change anything, and the fix for each one.
author: Jennifer Hudye

featuredImage.alt: Why Your Company Vision Isn't Working (And How to Fix It). Article by Jennifer Hudye of Vision Driven.

faq.q: Why do most company visions fail to change anything?
faq.a: Usually one of five reasons: it is too vague, it lives only in the founder's head, it is only about the business, it was written once and never revisited, or it was never connected to the quarterly plan.

faq.q: How do I know if my vision is too vague?
faq.a: Hand it to someone outside the company and ask them to describe your business in three years. If they can only give you adjectives back, it is too vague.

faq.q: How often should a vision be revisited?
faq.a: Read it out loud once a quarter before you plan the next ninety days, and rewrite it roughly once a year.

faq.q: Can a vision work if only the founder has seen it?
faq.a: No. If you are the only one who knows where the company is headed, you are also the only one who can make decisions, which defeats the purpose.

body:
Most founders have a vision. Most of those visions change nothing. The problem is almost never a lack of ambition. It is one of five specific failures, and each one has a fix.

1. It is too vague to act on

A vision full of words like world-class, mission-driven, and high-growth gives your team nothing to build. Nobody can picture world-class. They can picture we ship every project two days early and clients renew without asking the price.

Fix: rewrite every abstract line as a specific scene, number, or named outcome. Read Vivid Vision examples for the pattern.

2. It lives only in your head

If the clearest version of the vision is the one you carry around unspoken, your team is guessing. And a team that is guessing brings every decision back to you.

Fix: write it down in full, three to five pages, then run a real rollout. There is a walkthrough in getting your leadership team bought in.

3. It is only about the business

Most planning fixes your business or your personal life, but rarely both. A vision that says nothing about your health, your family, or your calendar will not survive a hard quarter, because there is nothing personal pulling you through it.

Fix: put your life in the same document as the revenue, with the same level of detail.

4. You wrote it once and never looked at it again

A vision you open once a year is a poster. It is not changing your Tuesday.

Fix: read it out loud once a quarter, by yourself, before planning the next ninety days. Rewrite it once a year.

5. It was never connected to the plan

A three year picture with nothing linking it to this week does not drive decisions. It just sits above the work, admired and ignored.

Fix: every quarter, break one slice of the vision into a real 90-day goal. That is the whole point of turning your vision into a plan.

How to diagnose which failure is yours

Run this quick check on your current vision.

  • Can someone outside the company read it and describe your business in three years? If not, it is too vague.
  • Has your team seen the full document and talked about it? If not, it lives only in your head.
  • Does it describe your health, family, and calendar in the same detail as revenue? If not, it is only about the business.
  • Have you read it out loud in the last 90 days? If not, you wrote it once and stopped.
  • Did this quarter’s plan include a goal drawn directly from the vision? If not, it is not connected to the plan.

Most stuck visions fail two or three of these at once. Fix them in order: specificity first, then rollout, then the personal section, then the rhythm, then the link to the quarter.

What a working vision feels like

Six months after fixing these, a few things change. Your team references the vision in decisions without you bringing it up. New hires get walked through it in week one. The questions coming to you get bigger and rarer. And you can describe where the company is going, out loud, without opening a document.

If none of that is happening yet, you have not fixed the failures. You have just rewritten the words.

The pattern

Notice that four of the five fixes are about what you do after the vision is written. Founders overestimate the writing and underestimate the sharing and the maintenance.

A rough vision that gets rolled out and revisited beats a beautiful one that lives in a drawer, every time. If you are starting over, use how to write a Vivid Vision.

The failure that hides the other four

There is a sixth failure worth naming, because it disguises itself as the others: the vision does not actually reflect what you want.

Some founders write a vision full of growth and scale because that is what a serious founder is supposed to want, while the quiet truth is they want a smaller, calmer, more profitable company and more time at home. A vision built on what you think you should want will never pull you, because part of you is not actually going there.

If your vision keeps failing to motivate you no matter how you fix the wording, sit with this one. Read the life section again. Ask whether it describes a life you genuinely want or a life you think you are supposed to want. The gap between those two is where a lot of dead visions come from.

How to restart a stalled vision

If your current vision has clearly failed, do not try to patch it. Set it aside and draft a fresh one, by hand, in two hours, using the prompt questions. Then compare the two. The differences tell you what was missing or dishonest in the first one.

Roll the new one out properly this time. Read it to your team live. Ask them what they want to own. Follow up within a week. Then read it yourself every quarter and connect one slice of it to your 90-day plan. That sequence is what separates a vision that works from one that decorates a folder.

Hold the vision. Not the circumstances.

title: Questions to Ask Before You Write Your Company Vision
metaTitle: Questions to Ask Before Writing Your Vision
metaDescription: The questions that pull a real Vivid Vision out of you, and the one question to avoid asking too early.
description: The questions that pull a real Vivid Vision out of you, and the one question to avoid asking too early.
author: Jennifer Hudye

featuredImage.alt: Questions to Ask Before You Write Your Company Vision. Article by Jennifer Hudye of Vision Driven.

faq.q: What is the one question to avoid when writing a vision?
faq.a: How. Asking how too early shrinks the vision down to whatever feels achievable today. Write the picture first. The how comes after.

faq.q: Should I answer these questions alone or with my team?
faq.a: Draft your answers alone first so they are honest. Then bring your leadership team in during the Expander stage to push the vision further.

faq.q: How long should this take?
faq.a: A focused couple of hours for a rough first pass. The full facilitated process takes a day plus a few weeks of refinement.

faq.q: What if I get stuck on a question?
faq.a: Skip it and come back. The questions about a normal day and about what your team does without you tend to open up the rest.

body:
A blank page is the enemy of a good vision. The fix is a set of questions that pull the picture out of you one piece at a time.

Answer these in the present tense, three years out. Write by hand or talk them through out loud.

About your day

  • What does a normal Tuesday look like? Where are you, what are you doing, and what are you not doing anymore?
  • What time do you start and stop? How many days a week do you work?
  • What is the first thing you do when you open your laptop?

About your team

  • Who is on your team, and what are they handling without checking with you?
  • What does a new hire say about their first week?
  • What decision would your team have brought to you last year that they now make on their own?

About your clients

  • How do clients describe you to a friend, word for word?
  • How do new clients find you?
  • What do you no longer have to explain or defend on a sales call?

About the money

  • What is the profit margin, not just the revenue?
  • How many months of cash are in the bank?
  • What does the business pay you, and what is that money doing for your life?

About your life

  • What does your health look like? What have you kept up for three straight years?
  • Where have you traveled, and who was with you?
  • What family moments did you not miss?

About the business, part two

  • What is the one thing people in your industry now say about your company that they did not used to say?
  • What did you stop selling, and why did that make the business better?
  • What is running smoothly now that used to be a weekly fire?
  • Who joined the team in the last three years that changed everything, and what do they own?

About your state of mind

  • How do you feel when you open your laptop on a normal work day?
  • What are you no longer worried about that used to keep you up?
  • What are you proud of that has nothing to do with revenue?
  • When someone asks how the business is going, what do you actually say, and how do you feel saying it?

How to answer these well

Say the answers out loud or write them by hand. Typing invites editing, and editing shrinks the vision.

Answer in the present tense, as if the three years have passed. Be specific enough that you could picture a real scene. And when you catch yourself hedging with roughly or hopefully, cross it out. If it is in the vision, it happened.

You do not have to answer every question. The ones about a normal day, and about what your team does without you, tend to open up the rest.

The question to save for later

Notice that none of these ask how. That is on purpose.

How is the question that shrinks a vision. The moment you ask how, your brain answers with whatever looks possible from where you stand today, and the vision collapses down to a slightly better version of now.

Write the whole picture first. Push it further in the Expander stage. Then, and only then, start asking how you get there and break it into a 90-day plan.

What to do when an answer will not come

Some questions will produce a blank. That blank is information, not a failure.

If you cannot describe what clients say about you in three years, you may not have decided what you want to be known for. If you cannot picture your team without you in it, you may be more attached to being needed than you thought. Note the blank and move on. Come back to it after the easier sections are filled, and the answer is often clearer.

Do this alone first, then with your team

Answer every question by yourself before you bring anyone else in. If you brainstorm the vision with your leadership team from a blank page, you get a safe, committee version that excites no one, including you.

Your draft should be yours. Then you bring your leaders in to stretch it, argue with it, and add what you missed. That order matters. See getting your leadership team bought in.

A shortcut for the personal section

Founders freeze on the life questions more than the business ones. If that is you, try this. Describe a single perfect ordinary day three years from now, hour by hour, from waking up to going to sleep. Where are you. Who is there. What do you do in the morning. When do you start work and when do you stop. What is dinner like.

A day is concrete enough to actually write, and once you have one, the rest of the life section tends to fall out of it.

Hold the vision. Not the circumstances.

title: How to Get Your Leadership Team Bought Into the Vision
metaTitle: Getting Your Leadership Team Bought Into the Vision
metaDescription: How to bring your leadership team into the Vivid Vision so they own it, speak to it in their own words, and roll it out to their people.
description: How to bring your leadership team into the Vivid Vision so they own it, speak to it in their own words, and roll it out to their people.
author: Jennifer Hudye

featuredImage.alt: How to Get Your Leadership Team Bought Into the Vision. Article by Jennifer Hudye of Vision Driven.

faq.q: Should my leadership team help write the Vivid Vision?
faq.a: You draft the first version so it is genuinely yours. Then you bring your leadership team in during the Expander stage to push it further and pressure-test it. They should shape it, not start it.

faq.q: What if a leader disagrees with part of the vision?
faq.a: Good. Hear it fully. Either their point improves the vision, or the conversation surfaces a real misalignment you needed to know about before you rolled it out to the whole company.

faq.q: How do I know my leaders actually own it?
faq.a: They can describe the vision in their own words, without the document in front of them, and they bring it up in decisions without you prompting them.

faq.q: How does this scale past a small team?
faq.a: At larger sizes, the vision travels through your leaders. You align them deeply, then each of them rolls it out to their part of the company.

body:
A Vivid Vision that only you believe in is a hobby. A Vivid Vision your leadership team owns is how the company actually changes direction.

Getting from the first to the second is a specific process, and skipping it is why most vision rollouts land flat.

Draft it yourself first

The first version should be yours, written alone, in your voice. If you design it by committee from the start, it comes out safe and generic, and nobody feels it, including you.

Bring leaders in to push it, not to start it

Once you have a draft, sit with your leadership team and run the Expander conversation. For every section, ask: what are we missing, what is too small, and what would make this a vision worth three years of our lives?

Their job is to stretch it and pressure-test it. If a leader pokes a hole, that is a gift. Either the vision gets better, or you just found a misalignment you needed to know about before the whole company heard it.

Let them argue with it

If a leader disagrees with a part of the vision, do not smooth it over. Slow down and hear the whole objection. Some of the best lines in a Vivid Vision come from a leader saying that is not ambitious enough or that would make my team miserable.

You want the disagreement now, in a room, not six months from now in a hallway.

The ownership test

You know your leaders own the vision when they can describe it in their own words, without the document, and when they start referencing it in decisions without you bringing it up.

If they still say your vision instead of our vision, you are not done.

The Expander conversation with your leaders

When you sit down with your leadership team to push the draft, use a simple structure. Go section by section, and for each one ask three questions:

  • What are we missing here that has to be true in three years?
  • Where is this too small? Where are we protecting the current version of the company instead of the one we want?
  • What in here would make your team’s life worse, and how do we fix that now?

Write down every answer. Some of the strongest lines in a finished Vivid Vision come from a leader saying that is not ambitious enough or my team would hate that.

What to do when a leader will not get on board

Occasionally a leader hears the vision and cannot get behind it, even after a real conversation. That is important information, and it is better to have it now.

Sometimes their objection improves the vision and they come around. Sometimes it surfaces that they want a different company than the one you are building. Either way, do not roll the vision out to the whole company while a key leader is quietly against it. The team will feel the split.

Then it travels through them

Once your leaders own it, they roll it out to their parts of the company. You do not personally deliver the vision to all fifty people. You deliver it to your six leaders so deeply that they can carry it the rest of the way.

That is how a vision scales without getting watered down. For the full rollout sequence, see how to roll out your Vivid Vision, and for how it connects to execution, turn your vision into a plan.

Signs your leaders do not actually own it

  • They still call it your vision, not our vision.
  • They can only describe it by reading from the document.
  • They do not reference it in their own team meetings.
  • When a decision comes up that the vision clearly answers, they still bring it to you.

If you see these, the problem is not your team. It is that the vision was handed to them finished instead of shaped with them. Go back and run the Expander conversation properly, and give them real room to change it.

What buy-in looks like when it is real

A leader who owns the vision will argue for it in a room you are not in. They will turn down an opportunity because it does not fit the picture. They will use it to say no to their own team’s pet projects. They will bring you a decision already made, framed as here is what I did and why it fits where we are going.

That is the goal. Not agreement in a meeting. Leaders who carry the vision into the parts of the company you never see.

Keeping leaders aligned over time

Buy-in decays. People get busy, priorities shift, and a vision that was alive in Q1 can go quiet by Q3. Build a standing habit: every quarterly planning session opens with the leadership team reading the vision out loud together, before anyone sets a rock. Ten minutes. It re-aligns the people whose alignment matters most.

Hold the vision. Not the circumstances.

title: How to Roll Out Your Vivid Vision to a Remote Team
metaTitle: Rolling Out a Vivid Vision to a Remote Team
metaDescription: A step-by-step way to share your company vision with a distributed team so everyone sees the same picture at the same time.
description: A step-by-step way to share your company vision with a distributed team so everyone sees the same picture at the same time.
author: Jennifer Hudye

featuredImage.alt: How to Roll Out Your Vivid Vision to a Remote Team. Article by Jennifer Hudye of Vision Driven.

faq.q: Can a Vivid Vision rollout work for a fully remote team?
faq.a: Yes. Some of the strongest rollouts have been remote teams who received a printed vision packet in the mail and opened it together on a video call. The key is that everyone experiences it at the same time.

faq.q: Should I send the document ahead of time?
faq.a: No. Read it out loud together first, live. Send the written copy afterward. Reading it cold on their own is not the same experience.

faq.q: How long should a remote rollout meeting be?
faq.a: Sixty to ninety minutes. Twenty minutes to read it out loud, the rest for reactions and for people to claim the parts they want to own.

faq.q: What do I do after the meeting?
faq.a: Follow up within a week with each person about the part of the vision they raised their hand for, and put the one page Vivid Vision Blueprint somewhere the team sees it often.

body:
Rolling out a vision in a room is easy. Everyone feels the same energy at the same time. Doing it well with a team spread across five time zones takes a little more design, but it works.

Why the rollout is the whole point
